title: Grasping for more vs. giving it away
core: All of these track the movement of money, goods, or advantage relative to the self — either pulled inward or pushed outward — and almost all of them carry a verdict on the person doing the moving. The confusion isn't across the divide (nobody mixes up greed with giving); it's *within* each side, where the words differ not in direction but in what they specify: whether desire is settled or predatory, whether the object belongs to someone else, whether a duty is for sale, whether the gift is large, permanent, motive-pure, or handed down from a height. The two halves are also not clean mirrors — the taking words range from neutral to damning, while the giving words range from admiring to quietly contemptuous of the receiver.

words.nuance: The coldest and only redeemable member of the taking side: a settled habit of accumulating, with no victim and no moral sentence attached. It's the one you can say approvingly — an **acquisitive** firm, an **acquisitive** mind — which none of the others allow.

Money specifically, and the *hoarding* end of it — the miser who clutches, not the predator who seizes. **Avaricious** needs no power at all; a penniless clerk can be avaricious, whereas rapacity requires something to grab with.
The top of the scale, and the only one that implies a stripped victim. Where avarice keeps, **rapacious** takes — it presumes leverage (conquerors, creditors, landlords) and is purely condemnatory.

The only verb, and the only one about pure inward desire — nothing has been acquired, and nothing need ever be. Its defining restriction is ownership: what you **covet** is already somebody else's. Note the participle flips clean positive: *the coveted prize*.
Not about wanting money — about having a price. **Venal** requires an office with a duty to betray (judge, inspector, journalist); it names the mechanism of corruption, not the appetite behind it.

Money hasn't corrupted a duty here, it has *replaced a motive* — loyalty, conviction, love of the work. Nothing illegal need happen: a **mercenary** lawyer is perfectly lawful, just hollow, which is why the word cuts hardest applied to artists, athletes, and friends.

The only giving word that is a claim about *motive*, and an absolute one: cost to you, zero return. Scale and status are irrelevant — a stranger donating a kidney qualifies, a patron endowing a wing may not. That absoluteness is why the word so often arrives pre-loaded with suspicion.
Pure praise, measured in *size* — the gift is enormous and the giver has standing. Says nothing about why he gave; a munificent donor may be buying his name onto a building.

Points at deeds already done and benefits actually conferred — the ward is funded, not merely contemplated. It describes an agent as a standing character (patron, monarch, foundation), which is what makes it so easy to turn ironic. Distinguish *benevolent* (kindly intent) and *beneficial* (things that do good).

The only noun, and the only giving word with a built-in height difference: it flows downward and everyone knows the tap can be shut. It reliably sours in print, and the sneer lands on the *receiver* — "living on his father's largesse."

Specifies the mechanism: a permanent principal given to an institution, generating income forever. Uniquely, its second sense has no human giver at all — **endowed** with perfect pitch means nature or luck handed it over, unearned.

exam_note: The exam plays on the fact that neither side is uniform — it will offer *acquisitive* where the sentence demands a victim (needs *rapacious*) or *avaricious* where a duty is being sold (needs *venal*); watch too for the positive *coveted*, and never confuse **venal** (bribable) with **venial** (a forgivable sin).
